abstract: LLM agents that analyse tables on their own fail in two ways. A visible failure (a crash, an error, an empty answer) is caught and retried. A silent failure returns a clean, confident, wrong answer that looks exactly like a right one. We built AgentRel, a measurement layer that runs a local agent (qwen3:8b) over 50 question templates on five datasets in three topologies, labels all 750 runs against deterministic ground truth, learns to predict silent failure from data and trace features, and injects faults to measure how each topology degrades. 39.6% of runs failed, and 85% of those failures were silent. A class-weighted LightGBM gate scores runs by risk: out of fold it reaches PR-AUC 0.70 against a 0.40 base rate (ROC-AUC 0.77), and re-checking only the 20% highest-scored runs catches 40% of all failures, twice what random review catches. The signal is trace effort: failing runs make more tool calls and spend more tokens. Under fault injection every topology degrades significantly; orchestrator-worker holds up best (mean +20 points) and single ReAct worst (+31), mostly through tool failures. Corrupted tool output, the fault that manufactures silent failures, hurts all three topologies equally, because no topology checks values rather than steps.
model_choice: Four local 8B-class models were benchmarked on the same 150 runs before the corpus was built (Table 3). llama3 answered 39% of runs without calling a tool, inventing numbers instead of computing them, and failed most often. llama3.1:8b failed least, but hit the 12-step cap on a quarter of its runs and took 28 s a run. qwen3:8b with thinking turned off failed 48% against llama3.1's 44%, a gap well inside the noise of 150 runs from 41 templates, while running in 60% of the time and looping half as often; with thinking on it spends about 300 tokens a step on hidden reasoning. We chose qwen3:8b. The temperature is 0 and every run starts a fresh session.
failure_rates: A monitor that watches for errors would have seen 46 of the 297 failures. Failure rises with the task: 31% on the missingness table, 49% on the three-table Olist schema that needs joins (Figure 2). Seven of the 50 templates failed on every run and 16 never failed, so most of the variation is between questions, not between topologies. The topologies differ less in how often they fail than in how: single ReAct gives no usable answer on 9% of its runs, mostly by hitting the step cap, against 4-5% for the other two. Adding a planner, an inspector or peers turns those visible failures into silent ones: 90% of orchestrator-worker failures and 88% of peer tool-graph failures were silent, against 75% for single ReAct.
classifier: On seven templates it never saw, the class-weighted LightGBM ranks runs well above chance: PR-AUC 0.63 against the 0.30 a random ranker gets, and well above logistic regression (0.45), so the signal is non-linear. SMOTE before LightGBM scored slightly higher (0.67); with seven test templates the difference is within noise, and class weighting was kept as planned because it does not synthesise traces that no agent produced. The thresholded numbers need care. The F2 threshold chosen on validation is 0.11, which flags most runs: recall 97%, precision 41%. Flagging every run already scores F2 0.68, because at a 30-40% failure rate F2 rewards recall so heavily that 'flag everything' is a strong baseline. F2 alone therefore cannot show that the gate works; the ranking metrics and the review budget below are the evidence. The Brier score (0.231) equals the always-predict-the-base-rate dummy: class weighting pushes scores toward the extremes, so p̂ ranks well but is not yet a probability. Because a seven-template test fold is small, Table 7 repeats the evaluation on all 750 runs out of fold.
metrics: Out of fold, the gate's ranking holds up: PR-AUC 0.70 and ROC-AUC 0.77, with template-resampled intervals that stay well clear of the 0.40 base rate. The gate is most useful as a review queue. Re-checking the top 10% of runs catches 20% of all failures (a perfect ranker could catch 25%); the top 20% catches 40% (perfect: 51%); the top 30% catches 53% (perfect: 76%). Random review catches 10%, 20% and 30%. The out-of-fold F2 threshold, by contrast, degenerates: at θ = 0.04 it flags 84% of runs, so MCC (0.32) and balanced accuracy (0.62) are modest. A team that wants a fixed hold rule should pick θ by review capacity instead: at θ = 0.5 the gate holds 38% of runs, 62% of the held runs are failures, and it catches 61% of failures. Calibration is the weak point (ECE 0.16, Figure 4): half the runs score below 0.31 and a quarter above 0.80, more extreme than the observed failure rates, so p̂ should be recalibrated (for example by isotonic regression on held-out runs) before it is read as a chance. Figure 5 shows what the gate reads: the number of tool calls, prompt and completion tokens and wall time carry most of the gain, ahead of the question type and the data's shape. Failing runs work harder; the gate is detecting an agent that is struggling.
robustness: Every one of the nine cells degrades, and every confidence interval excludes zero. Orchestrator-worker is the most robust (mean +20 points), peer tool-graph next (+23) and single ReAct the least (+31). Most of single ReAct's deficit is one fault: a failing tool raises its failure rate from 31% to 80% (+49), because a lone loop with one retry spends its step budget on the broken tool, whereas the orchestrator's inspector and worker redo absorb the same fault (+16); these two intervals do not overlap. Corrupted output hurts all three topologies almost equally (+28 to +31 points, overlapping intervals) and turns runs into silent failures: 44% of corrupted-output runs ended in a confident wrong value, against 24% at baseline, while visible failures stayed near 8% under every fault. The inspector checks that steps ran, not that their values are right, so a quietly wrong number passes every topology. Dropped context is the mildest fault (+12 to +20). Outside tool failure, the topologies' intervals overlap, so their ranking on the other two faults is not established at this sample size (49 questions; 77% of injected faults fired before the agent answered).
relate: The gate predicts failure about equally well in every topology (out-of-fold PR-AUC 0.69-0.73, lift 1.7-1.9x over each topology's failure rate), and in every topology a per-topology model draws about three quarters of its gain from the dynamic trace block and only 5-7% from the graph block. So the most robust topology is not the one whose failures are easiest to predict; robustness and predictability are largely independent here, which is useful in practice, because one gate serves all three topologies without retuning. Scored on fault runs it never trained on, the gate's ranking transfers: PR-AUC is above each cell's failure rate everywhere (0.78-0.95), including corrupted output (0.89-0.92 against failure rates of 0.61-0.72). The recall column of Table 9 is near 100% only because the out-of-fold F2 threshold flags most runs (false-alarm rates of 69-100%), so it says little on its own; the ranking is the result.
discussion: Silent failure is the common case, not the edge case. 251 of 297 failures returned a clean answer. Any reliability measure built on exceptions, error logs or retries sees about one failure in six. More agent structure makes this worse, not better: the multi-agent topologies trade crashes for confident wrong answers.

Trace effort is a cheap, model-agnostic warning signal. Tool calls, tokens and time are logged by every agent framework already, are available before the answer is shown, and carry most of the gate's signal in all three topologies. The gate needs no access to the model's weights or log-probabilities.

Use the gate as a review queue, not a yes/no classifier. At a 30-40% failure rate an F2-optimal threshold flags almost everything. The deployable form is Algorithm 3's batch mode: review the k% highest-scored runs, where the top 20% holds twice its share of failures.

Inspectors inspect steps, not values. Corrupted output degraded every topology equally, including the one with an inspector. A value-level check, such as recomputing a result by a second route or testing it against simple bounds, is the missing component, and the gate's ranking already says which runs deserve one.
Topology matters most when tools break. Orchestrator-worker absorbed tool failures that single ReAct did not; for the other faults the choice of topology made no measurable difference.
limitations: One base model. All numbers are for qwen3:8b at temperature 0 on a laptop. Larger models will fail less, and possibly differently; the framework runs unchanged on any Ollama model.

Scale and synthetic data. Three of the five datasets are seeded synthetic stand-ins, there are 50 templates, and the held-out test fold has only seven. The template-resampled intervals are wide for that reason, and the out-of-fold evaluation in Table 7 is the better estimate.

A strict tolerance. Eq. (1) allows 1% relative error. 30 runs (4% of the corpus) were 1-5% off, mostly rounding; a looser tolerance would lower the failure rate by about four points without changing the conclusions.

Wall time is partly contaminated. The machine slept for several hours while the corpus was generated, which inflated the wall time of roughly 20 runs. The IQR cap (52 s) bounds their effect, and the token and tool-call counts, which sleep cannot affect, carry the same signal, but wall_time_s should be read with that in mind.
Scores are not calibrated probabilities (ECE 0.16), and the gate scores finished runs: it can hold an answer before a user sees it, but it is not yet an early warning during a run.
The fault study uses the canonical phrasing only and one fault per run; the 23% of injected faults that never fired are excluded rather than counted as survived.
conclusion: Silent failure is the main way a local LLM data-analysis agent goes wrong: 85% of failures in our corpus returned a clean answer that nothing flagged. Both research questions have a positive, if bounded, answer. (Q1) Features of the execution trace predict silent failure well above chance on unseen questions, and the resulting gate, used as a review queue, finds twice as many failures as random checking for the same effort. (Q2) Topology matters: orchestrator-worker is the most robust and single ReAct the least, mostly because of how each handles a failing tool, but no topology resists corrupted output, the fault that produces silent failures. The next step is the one both results point to: a value-level check inside the agent, applied first to the runs the gate ranks highest.
